title: The stick in the fire
hookLine: a stick that tends a fire until the fire takes the stick
carry: every thought hangs on the thought 'i'

lines: AT THE END, THE STICK BURNS TOO.
cards: At a cremation fire, someone tends the flames with a long stick, pushing the wood in, turning it so it burns through. It's a plain, sober job. And at the end, when everything has burned, the stick goes into the fire too.
Ramana Maharshi takes that stick and puts it in the middle of Who Am I? It's his answer to a question the text raises plainly: what do you do with all these thoughts?

teach.h: TO WHOM DID THIS THOUGHT COME? TO ME.
teach.b: His advice is short. When a thought comes up, don't follow it, and don't argue with it. Instead ask: to whom did this thought come?
The answer arrives on its own: to me. Then ask: and who am I? That turns the mind back toward where it came from, he says, and the thought fades.
Do it again with the next one. Here's why it works, in his account.

teach.h: EVERY THOUGHT HANGS ON THE THOUGHT 'I'.
teach.b: All the other thoughts hang on one thought: the thought I. Hindu teachers have an old name for that I-maker: ahankara, the ego. Worries, plans, memories, all of them belong to someone.
Follow the I back toward its source, and the rest has nothing to hang on. This is atma-vichara, inquiry into the self, Ramana's whole method.

teach.h: THE STICK BURNS AT THE END TOO.
teach.b: So the question does the job of the stick, turning the other thoughts into the fire. And at the end, Ramana says, it burns up too. Even the question doesn't stay.
Somebody asks whether a seeker first needs to study all the tattvas, the categories philosophers say make up the world and the person. Ramana says no.
If you want to throw out the garbage, you don't need to analyze it first. In his account, you don't have to map everything you are not before you ask who you are. You only have to ask.

how: In self-inquiry as Ramana taught it, people meet each passing thought with 'to whom did this come?' and turn back toward the sense of 'I', in sitting practice and through the day.

o: a priest who tended the cremation fires of a town
a teacher who said to follow every thought to its end
the sage who said: ask to whom each thought came

p: to whom did this thought come?
what every other thought hangs on

s: Ramana says you must study and count every category of reality before you can inquire
he says you don't need to analyze garbage before throwing it out.
in the text, the question 'who am I?' itself burns up in the end
like the stick used to stir a cremation fire, which goes into the fire at the end.
Ramana's advice is to follow each thought to see where it leads
he says not to follow it, but to ask to whom it came.

games.q: why does asking 'to whom did this come?' quiet the other thoughts, in Ramana's account?
o: it's a distraction, like counting sheep.
every thought hangs on the thought 'I'; follow that back, and they have nothing to hang on.
it proves the thought wrong, so it leaves.
games.why: for Ramana, the I-thought, the ego, comes first and the rest hang on it. turn toward its source and the others fade; at the end, like the stick, even the question burns up.

practice: Wait for the first thought, which won't take long, and instead of following its story, ask quietly: to whom did this come?

Let the answer be there, to me, then ask who am I, and let the attention turn back toward the one asking, resting there until the next thought arrives, and then again. If you pray, you can let this turning home be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Ramana Maharshi. The teacher who said: when a thought comes, ask to whom it came, then ask who am I, and let the question burn up like the stick in the fire.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: aham, 'I'. Ramana teaches that every other thought hangs on the thought 'I'.

carryVoice: Your line: every thought hangs on the thought 'i'. Tomorrow, the helps Ramana allows along the way: the breath, a name of God, and an elephant. Day nine hundred fifty, done.
